p: Saturday, September 25, Maria had the car keys in her hand and the garage door halfway up when her phone buzzed again.
A text from Nate Ostrowski. Bridge is open. I've activated the incident response plan, and I'm incident commander. The clinic manager is on with me now. Need you on patient care. Do not drive up yet.

She read the last line twice. Rawlins was three hours away. A year ago she'd have been past Wellington before anybody could text her anything, laptop on the passenger seat, badge in her teeth. She'd have walked into the clinic before noon and been the most senior person in a building that needed a network engineer.

She stood there while the door finished going up. Then she pressed the button again and watched it come down, and hung the keys on their hook, and went in to the kitchen table. That was where the bridge call would live for the next three days.
Before she dialed in, she called Joan. It was 8:19, and Joan picked up on the second ring.
Lucia's mug from last Sunday was still in the drying rack. Twenty-one days, Maria thought, and dialed in.

Nate ran the bridge the way he'd once run a radio net, in short sentences, with every name written down. A dozen people were on by 8:31. The clinic manager was on her cell in the parking lot, because Nate had told her to step outside and stay off the clinic's phones. She read him the note off the front desk screen a second time, slowly, so his deputy could type it.

What the screen said. Your network has been encrypted. We have copied your files. To recover them, and to keep them from being published, contact us within seventy-two hours at the address below. Do not contact police. Do not try to restore your files yourself.

Nate had the incident response plan open, the one his team had rewritten in the spring and walked through at a tabletop exercise in June. Maria had been at the tabletop for an hour, then left early for a One Chart meeting.
Gail was on the line from the hospital across town. My clinic has eleven walk-ins in the waiting room and a sign on the door, she said. Somebody tell me what my people do.

Maria says it out loud on the bridge, so it's in Nate's log. Nate is incident commander. Joan owns the privacy questions and is on by 8:40. Cascade's general counsel joins at nine. The risk manager notifies the insurer before ten, the way the policy says. Maria owns patient care. By 9:15 the walk-ins are seeing a nurse practitioner in the hospital's outpatient wing, on hospital computers, with paper downtime forms. The clinic stays dark. Gail reads the plan's roles page out loud to her managers. So I don't have to know everything. Nobody does. That's why it has a page.

At 9:05 Nate put the map on the bridge's shared screen. The clinic had a small server in a back closet, eighteen computers, and a link across town to the Rawlins hospital, which connected to Fort Collins and everything Cascade ran. The clinic's charts lived in Corvane, in Fort Collins, and Corvane looked untouched. So did the hospital. So far.
Marcus had joined without being asked. Relay's seeing normal traffic from the hospital, he said. Nothing from the clinic since 7:58. I'm watching.
The clinic manager asked what any clinic manager would. Should we just turn everything off?

Nate's network engineer cuts the clinic's link at the hospital end at 9:11 and shuts off the clinic's remote access gateway. The clinic manager walks the building pulling network cables, every one, and leaves every machine running with its note glowing, so whatever is in memory stays put. Nate's team disables every account that signed in at the clinic this month. Then they watch the hospital's network, the Corvane sign-ins, and Marcus's feeds, hour by hour. Nothing crosses. Still quiet, Marcus says at noon, and at two, and at six.

By evening the clinic was an island and the hospital was still running. The price of that was in Tasha's queue. Nate's team had disabled every account that had signed in at the clinic in the last thirty days, forty-six of them, and fourteen belonged to hospital staff who covered the clinic's Saturday walk-ins. Each reset needed the person on video with their badge. Tasha's desk had forty-one tickets by eleven.
At 11:40 the Rawlins ED charge nurse called Maria directly. The night doctor and two of her nurses couldn't sign in to Corvane, and a man with chest pain was in room two.
Give me one login for the department tonight. One. I'll keep it on a card at the desk, and you can kill it at seven. Tasha, still on the bridge: Forty minutes each, at the rate we're verifying.

The house supervisor opens the safe. The emergency accounts are there, one sealed envelope each, a page from the downtime procedures rebuilt after the survey last fall. The doctor and both nurses sign the log with their own names beside the envelope numbers and are in the chart by 11:52. The man in room two gets his troponin read at 12:20. By seven the help desk has reset all fourteen, the emergency accounts are off, and Nate's team reads every chart they opened: nine, every one an ED patient. Tasha closes the last ticket at 7:14 and sends one line. Envelopes worked.

Sunday, September 26, at nine, the bridge turned into a meeting with a door. Cascade's general counsel sat in the Fort Collins conference room with the CEO, Ochoa, Nate, Joan, and Maria. Gail and the risk manager were on the speaker.

Nate's team knew what they knew. The clinic's server and computers were encrypted. Corvane was clean. The firewall log showed a large transfer out of the clinic late Thursday night, so the note's claim that they'd copied files was probably true. The deadline on the note ran out Monday morning.
The CEO asked what everyone had been carrying since Saturday. What does it cost to just pay it? Three weeks before we move three hospitals, I'd like this over.

Counsel lays it out, and the room agrees in twenty minutes. Paying buys a promise from people who've just shown what their promises are worth. It doesn't unsend a copy, and counsel has questions about whether paying some groups is legal at all. Cascade has backups. Nate calls the FBI's field office before ten, and an agent calls back within the hour. Joan's breach assessment starts today, whatever the note says. The insurer hears every step through the risk manager. The CEO nods slowly. So it isn't over. It's over when we've restored, told everyone we have to tell, and closed the hole.
At 3:10 that afternoon Joan's email went to the incident team.

An email from Joan Whitfield. Subject: Breach risk assessment. Starting the assessment today. We discovered this Saturday, September 25, at 8 AM, so the clock started Saturday. Under HIPAA, unauthorized access to patient data is presumed to be a breach unless we can show a low probability it was compromised. From Nate I need what was on the clinic server and whether it left. From everyone else I need no statements about what was or wasn't taken until I have that. Joan

Nate already had part of the answer. The clinic's computers held no chart, since that lived in Corvane. The server held scanned intake forms, a folder of reports, and shared drives nobody had cleaned out in years. At four, Corvane's security team emailed to say the chart was safe, so this probably wasn't a breach at all. Somebody forwarded it to Joan with a smiley face.

Joan runs it in the open, one page per factor. What data, and how identifying it is. Who has it: people who asked for money and threatened to publish. Whether it was taken: the firewall log says yes, about two gigabytes, Thursday night. How far it's mitigated: not far, yet. She asks Nate one more question: could anyone have known sooner? The firewall logged the transfer Thursday night, but nothing alerted on it and nobody could have read it before Saturday, so Saturday stands as discovery, and she writes down why. She marks her wall calendar in red on Wednesday, November 24, sixty days from discovery, and writes sooner beside it. The clock started when we found it, not when we finish understanding it, she says. So we work fast, and we say only what we know.
Sunday at 9:15 PM, Maria was still on the bridge from her kitchen table when Kiran texted.
A text from Kiran Bhatt. Marcus says you've been on the bridge since Saturday. It's Sunday. Who's your second?

She looked at it for a while. Nate's deputy had been on since six. She typed: Nate's deputy, till 6 AM. Kiran answered before she could put the phone down. Then hang up. You told me five. She muted the bridge and went to bed. On Monday's page, under KIRAN, the two small words from August were still there. She hadn't expected to need them on a Sunday.

Monday, September 27, at 6:30, Ochoa was in the Fort Collins conference room before anyone else, with a page of his legal pad already full: one statement for the board, the staff, and the papers. He'd been up since four writing it. Maria could read the first line from the door. The patient record was not affected. True, as far as it went.

The communications director had three requests waiting: a reporter from the Rawlins paper, staff across the system who'd heard something, and the board chair, who wanted Ochoa on the phone by eight. Ochoa uncapped his pen to sign his page. Then he looked at Maria, who'd spent two days on the bridge and knew what his first line left out, and capped it again. He tore the page off the pad, folded it twice, and put it in his inside pocket. You know what we know, he said. I've got an opinion. Write it, and I'll sign what you write.

Maria and the communications director write one page, and Joan and counsel read every line. A Cascade clinic in Rawlins was hit by ransomware Saturday. Its patients were moved and seen. The health record system wasn't affected. Whether patient information was taken is under investigation, and anyone whose information was will be told directly. Next update Wednesday at noon. Staff get it at nine, before anyone else. The board chair at 9:30, from Ochoa, reading Maria's page. The reporter at ten. Every manager gets the same page and the same line for questions they can't answer yet. Ochoa signs the bottom without changing a word. On his way out, he drops the folded page in the shred bin by the door.

Monday at two, Nate's team had a timeline. The first sign-in nobody could explain came through the clinic's remote access gateway on Friday, September 10, at 11:52 PM. The copy left Thursday night, September 23. The note went up early Saturday.

The restore was settled by three. The clinic's server was backed up every night, and on Sundays a copy also went to storage nobody could change or delete for thirty-five days. Corvane's project director wanted Friday night's backup, the newest, so the clinic could open Wednesday. Nate answered in one sentence: Friday's backup was two weeks younger than the intruder. His team would restore the locked copy from Sunday, September 5, on a network with no way out. They'd scan it, check its system files against known good copies, put two-factor sign-in on the gateway, and make every password that had touched the clinic new. What changed since the fifth would come back from the chart in Corvane and a box of paper intake forms the front desk had kept. The vice president for clinics, who owned the clinic's systems, would sign before it reconnected. The clinic would open Saturday, a week after it closed.
Nate's team had restored a clinic server from a locked copy once, in June, as a test. It had taken six hours, and they'd written down every step.

At 3:20 Maria's phone buzzed under the table. Lucia. Rawlins is on the radio. Are you ok? Then a second one. Does it move the 16th? It wasn't a question about an EHR. Maria typed: Not if I can help it. The answer came back in seconds. Nineteen days.

That left the part nobody had said yet. Maria put a finger on the first line of the timeline. Eleven fifty-two on the tenth. Was that in a log? The gateway logged it, Nate said. It logged the copy going out, too. Fourteen days. Nobody reads that log unless something's already wrong. He didn't say it like an excuse. He said it like a finding.

Nate brings it to the security committee Friday, and Maria signs under him. Security reviews alerts on remote and after-hours sign-ins every morning, gateways first. The monthly scans keep running, and every finding goes to its owner with a date. Every quarter, each system's owner reviews who has remote or admin access and takes off what isn't needed. Once a year, and after any big change, an outside firm that built none of it runs a penetration test. Each quarter the committee gets a short report: what was checked, what was found, who owns each finding, and when it's due. In week three, before the first access review has run, the morning check catches a sign-in at 2:14 AM from a contractor whose contract ended in August. The account is off by 2:30. Fourteen days to sixteen minutes, Nate says. That's the job. The access review in January takes off ninety-four more.

Tuesday, September 28, the fourth day, Maria drove to Rawlins after all, because the insurer's investigator wanted to see the clinic and Nate wanted her there to answer for patient care. Nate met her in the parking lot with two coffees and a four-day beard. The paper sign was still taped inside the front door.

The investigator pulled in at 10:30, four hours up from Denver. Henry Ashby was somewhere in his forties, in a dark jacket that had spent the drive folded on a seat, with a hard-sided case in one hand. He looked tired in a way a night's sleep wasn't going to fix. He shook Nate's hand, then Maria's, and looked past them both into the clinic for a long moment before he said anything.

Morning. Henry Ashby, for the insurer. He set the case on the front desk. I'll want the logs and the images as your team preserved them. With the hashes, and a record of who's handled them since Saturday.

Nate, trying to help, offered him a login to the console so he could look at anything he liked. Kind of you. I'd rather not. He said it pleasantly. If I sign in, I'm part of your evidence. On the way past the back hall he'd glanced at the server closet, its door propped open with a rubber wedge because the little room ran hot. He didn't mention it. He wrote something in a bound notebook. Then he turned to Maria. One question. Who decided the backups were clean, and how?

Counsel has already cleared the handoff. Nate's deputy brings the drives with the custody log: each image, its hash, and every name and time it passed through since Saturday. Henry connects the first drive through a small gray write blocker from his case, so nothing on it can change, and computes the hash on his own laptop. He reads the digits out. Nate reads his. They match. Henry writes it in the notebook by hand, with the time, signs it, and turns the notebook around for Nate to sign under him. Then Maria answers. Nate's team decided, in writing: a locked copy from September 5, before the first unexplained sign-in, restored in isolation, scanned, and checked against known good files. The vice president for clinics signed for reconnecting. Henry writes that down too. Good, he says. That's the sentence I drove up for. He's on the road back to Denver by one.
Wednesday, September 29, Nate's team finished sorting what had left the clinic Thursday night. Most of it was old reports. One file wasn't.

It was a spreadsheet from October 2023, made for a flu shot mailing by a clinic manager who'd since moved to Casper. Four thousand one hundred eighty patients: names, birth dates, addresses, phone numbers, and insurance member numbers. It sat in a folder called Misc on the clinic's shared drive. Nobody had opened it in two years. Nobody owned it.

Joan read it standing up. That settles factor three, she said. Gail, on the speaker from the hospital, asked the next question. How many more of those are sitting on shared drives right now? Nobody knew. There were forty clinics.

Counsel puts a legal hold on everything from the Rawlins clinic, so nothing there is destroyed while it's evidence. For the other thirty-nine, the vice president for clinics is the owner, and each clinic's medical director answers for their own drives. Nate's team scans every share for patient data and sends each owner a list. Each file gets a classification, restricted for anything with patient data, and a fate under the retention schedule: move it into a governed system with access by role, or destroy it, shredded or wiped, with a record of what and when. By the end of October 187 files are gone, each with a line in a log. Joan reads the first owner's list and writes in the margin. Somebody finally owns Misc.

Thursday, September 30, Nate brought the ticket. The patch for the clinic's remote access gateway had come out in July. Nate's monthly scan flagged the gateway as critical on Monday, July 26, and the ticket went where tickets for Rawlins always went: to Dale, the hospital's one IT tech.

In August Dale had been pulled onto One Chart testing three days a week. The ticket sat in his queue for sixty-one days, marked critical, with nobody else watching it. Dale was on the call, and he hadn't slept much either. I saw it. I meant to get to it on a Friday. There weren't any Fridays.
Maria knew that sentence. She'd heard Kiran say it in August, in other words. And when she'd put every project and its people on one page in August, nobody's patching had been on it.

Nate and Maria put it on one page, and the IT steering committee approves it Friday. Nate's team scans every month and rates what it finds. Every system has a named owner, accountable for getting its findings fixed: critical within fourteen days, high within thirty. IT operations patches through change control. An owner who can't meet a deadline signs an exception with a compensating control and an end date. Anything late goes to Nate and Maria every Monday. Patching goes on the portfolio page as real work, with hours, so a project can't quietly eat it again. Dale gets a second tech for the Wyoming clinics, on loan from Fort Collins. So it's not just my queue. It never should've been.

Thursday afternoon, Nate's scan of the other thirty-nine clinics came back. Nine had the same gateway. Three had been patched in July by a contractor who happened to be on site that week. Six hadn't. The scan also listed 212 other findings across the clinics, most of them medium or low.
Corvane's project director wrote within the hour. Sixteen days to go-live, and the freeze started Monday, his email said. Please, nothing that isn't One Chart.
Brett called an hour later. He didn't argue for the freeze. Do what you need to, he said. I'll handle my side.

Nate ranks all 218 findings by likelihood and impact. The six gateways score 25, the top of the scale, and nothing else comes close. They go to an emergency change board that night, each with a tested back-out plan, and remote access at those six clinics stays off until each one is patched and has two-factor sign-in. Dale and the tech from Fort Collins patch two a night, Friday through Sunday. Monday's rescan shows all six fixed. The other 212 go on the normal schedule by score, each with an owner and a deadline. Corvane's director reads the emergency change record and writes back one line. Understood. That's a fix.

Friday, October 1, Maria walked the clinic with Gail and the clinic manager the day before it reopened. The computers were new, or new to the clinic. The screens were clean. Most of what she found wasn't on a screen.

The server closet door was propped open with a rubber wedge. Two front desk monitors faced the waiting room chairs. A sticky note under one keyboard held a password, the new one. And the clinic manager said, a little embarrassed, that the front desk had always stayed signed in all day under whoever came in first, because signing in took ninety seconds and the line didn't wait.
Every one of those is a person trying to get through a Saturday, Gail said. Don't fix them with a memo.

By Saturday at eight it's three kinds of fixes. Technical: two-factor on all remote access, a badge tap that signs a person in at the front desk in four seconds instead of ninety, every user under their own name, and screens that lock after a few idle minutes. Physical: a vent fan in the closet so the door can close and lock, a badge reader on it, and the front desk monitors turned away from the chairs, with privacy screens. Administrative: twenty minutes of training before the doors open, in the clinic manager's own words, and a sanctions policy everyone already had and has now read. Before the electrician wires the reader, Maria opens the closet and looks at every shelf. Switches, the new server, a box of printer paper. The downtime forms are in the front desk's bottom drawer, and that drawer has no lock on it. She leaves it that way. The sticky note goes in the shred bin. Gail watches the front desk nurse tap in. Four seconds. She'll do that.

Saturday, October 2, the Rawlins clinic opened for walk-ins at eight, a week to the day after the note. The front desk nurse signed in with a tap of her badge. Fourteen patients came before noon. One asked whether it was true about the computers, and the nurse handed her the page Maria had written, which had a third update on it by then.
Nate's Friday report had one line about the Rawlins ED. Nine charts opened on emergency accounts Saturday night, nine ED patients, every one reviewed by Sunday noon.

On Friday the steering committee had met for twenty minutes. One Chart's date held at October 16, with the go or no-go still ahead. Nate had asked for one thing in return and gotten it: the six gateways came first.

Maria made the list on the drive back from Rawlins, out of habit. Nate, the bridge. Joan, the clock. Counsel, the ransom. Dale, two gateways a night. Her own line was the shortest: patients seen, owners named, in bed Sunday when Kiran said so.

Sunday, October 3, Lucia called from Greeley at nine at night, which she never did. She'd had her first clinical day that week, at a nursing home in Evans, taking blood pressures with an instructor at her elbow. Nine residents. She'd written down every number twice. Then, before Maria could ask anything else: Thirteen days. Thirteen days. It didn't move? It didn't move. Lucia was quiet a second. Good. I was afraid it was going to be one more thing.

Monday, October 4, Henry's follow-up had come through counsel overnight. The hashes matched, the custody log was complete, and there was one observation: Tuesday, 10:34, server closet door held open with a rubber wedge. By then the door had been shut and locked since Saturday.

At 7:10 Joan came to Maria's office with the assessment in a blue folder. Four factors, one conclusion: a breach, 4,180 patients, all of them Wyoming residents. The letters would go out by October 15, weeks inside the sixty days, with the notice to Wyoming media and the report to HHS the same day, and credit monitoring for anyone who wanted it. She'd written every line herself.

Then she stood in the doorway a moment longer, folder against her chest. Saturday, 8:19, she said. Gail called you at 8:14. You called me before you'd even joined Nate's bridge. I was your first call this time. Joan doesn't smile at work, as a rule, and she almost did. I noticed.
